title: LP2-00–55: ordinary primes instead of primes minus one
question: Does uninterrupted prime arithmetic recover any of nine fixed 12-rune openings at the start of an LP2-00–55 page?
summary: Changing only the schedule to ordinary primes gives zero exact matches in 3190 candidates. Every output is one alphabet position from its baseline counterpart; these are related searches, not independent confirmations.

scope.representation: All recognized runes in archived order, including headings. Ignore other characters. Empty pages contribute no candidates.
scope.procedure: Apply prime shifts modulo 29, with both subtraction and addition. Compare the first 12 output indices with nine fixed known openings; retain full candidates.
scope.parameters: Offsets 0–28 inclusive; two directions; independent page reset; one term per rune; no interruptions. 55 rune-bearing pages, 3190 candidates, 28710 comparisons.
scope.exclusions: Other beginnings, offsets above 28, interruptions, heading removal, reversed input, word or row resets, cross-page carry, other numerical schedules and language scoring.

finding: Zero exact opening matches in 28710 comparisons. All 3190 candidate sequences reproduce, and every output equals the baseline plus the arithmetic direction modulo 29.
limitations: Only nine fixed initial openings and offsets 0–28. No general readability test. Ordinary primes and primes minus one differ by a constant output shift under these rules; do not count them as independent evidence. Computational review only; human review pending.
next_steps: Use the baseline relation to avoid duplicate work when trying all constant shifts. Other schedules, interruption rules or plaintext criteria need separately declared variants.

family.title: Numerical keystreams and known openings
family.question: Do declared numerical schedules recover fixed known openings under explicit offset and advancement rules?

variant.label: Ordinary primes; all other settings fixed

changes.before: Apply prime-minus-one shifts modulo 29, with both subtraction and addition. Compare the first 12 output indices with nine fixed known openings; retain full candidates.
changes.after: Apply prime shifts modulo 29, with both subtraction and addition. Compare the first 12 output indices with nine fixed known openings; retain full candidates.
changes.reason: Replace each prime-minus-one term with the corresponding prime. Preserve offsets, signs, advancement and opening criteria to isolate the schedule change.

review.reviewer: Codex — full rerun, trial-division audit and complete baseline comparison; human review pending

reproduction.environment: Python 3.12.10, standard library. Independent audit: python experiments/records/lp2-prime-openings/check.py

visuals.caption: Four saved LP2-00 candidate indices: changing to ordinary primes lowers every subtraction output by one modulo 29. Neither candidate is a known reading.

reader_finding: None of the 3,190 outputs from adding or subtracting successive primes began with any of nine known 12-rune openings.
reader_limit: Only the first 29 starting points were checked, without skips. Ordinary-prime and prime-minus-one shifts differ by a constant alphabet shift, so these are closely related tests.

browser_followups.question: Do outputs from the fixed prime-number stream resemble the maintained language samples across 29 starting places, both arithmetic directions and page, line or word restarts?
browser_followups.scope_change: Keep the original 29 starting places, addition and subtraction, and LP2-00-55. Include page restarts and add line and word restarts. Compare language samples instead of the nine fixed historical openings.
browser_followups.limitation: Use the stored 305-term sequence once per restart, without wrapping, skipped runes or carry between pages. These new comparisons have no results yet.
